answer: The BLIS 6-knob configuration space has a hierarchically structured Pareto front governed by four architecture-independent regularities: (1) TP dominance — higher tensor parallelism always yields better throughput at fixed GPU count, with the ratio scaling by model size (2.06x for 7B, 2.68x for 14B, 4.5x for 70B). (2) Effective cache equivalence — performance depends on kv_blocks × block_size, making block_size=16 strictly dominated by block_size=32 at same kv_blocks. (3) maxr=256 saturation plateau — maxr=512 never improves over 256. (4) Scheduler × concurrency interaction in degraded cache regimes only — SJF with reduced maxr creates distinct Pareto tradeoffs (2-7% higher rps at cost of higher tail latency) when cache pressure triggers preemptions. A v2 hierarchical search exploiting these regularities achieves 100% unique Pareto tuple recall at budget=100 (out of 1800 configs) on qwen3-14B/rate=100/seed=42, up from the v1 baseline of 80.0%. Three structural changes: selective Phase 2 (skip non-degrading combos at high kv, saves ~22 evals), eliminated Phase 3 (block_size=16 sweep, zero Pareto impact, saves 30 evals), expanded Phase 2.5 (probe all degraded combos including non-best-per-GPU). The v1 dead zone (80% recall at both budget=100 and 125) is eliminated. Pareto diversity scales with model size (21/35/42 tuples for 7B/14B/70B) and arrival rate (23/35/41 tuples at rate=50/100/200).
